Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National | Opinion Ghana’s galamsey crisis: The tragedy of the commons, market failure and the economics of environmental destruction Source : Nana Eghan, PhD 2 November 2026 11:21am Audio By Carbonatix
Why Ghana must move beyond enforcement to correct the economic incentives driving illegal mining.
Ghana's illegal gold mining crisis, popularly known as galamsey, is often treated primarily as an environmental or law-enforcement problem. Yet its persistence reveals a deeper economic failure: those extracting gold capture much of the income, while communities and taxpayers bear much of the cost.
Effective policy must therefore go beyond disrupting mining sites to changing the incentives that make environmental destruction profitable.
The Tragedy of the Commons In 1968, Garrett Hardin popularised the concept of the tragedy of the commons: individually rational exploitation can collectively degrade resources on which everyone depends. Ghana's rivers and watersheds illustrate the problem. A miner operating along the Pra River earns income from gold, but downstream households, farmers and water utilities bear the consequences of sedimentation and pollution.
The miner benefits from additional extraction without fully paying for the resulting damage. Multiplied across many operators, private gains can produce collective losses. Nevertheless, as Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom demonstrated, shared resources need not be destroyed: effective rules, community participation and credible monitoring can sustain them. Ghana's challenge is therefore as much institutional as environmental.
Private Profits, Public Costs Economists describe costs imposed on others but excluded from private decisions as negative externalities. Mining equipment, fuel and labour appear in an operator's accounts; polluted drinking water, damaged cocoa farms and future restoration costs often do not. This divergence can make environmentally destructive mining privately profitable even when its overall contribution to national welfare is negative.
A 2024 peer-reviewed study of selected Ghanaian farming communities found that 38% of surveyed farmers reported mining-related land degradation, while 79% of affected farmers reported that degraded areas had not been reclaimed. These are local findings, not national estimates, but they illustrate the erosion of productive assets.
In October 2026, the Government announced GH¢200 million for reclaiming 5,000 acres of mining-degraded land from 2027. Environmental restoration is essential. But why should taxpayers routinely pay to repair damage while private operators and financiers retain the proceeds?
When profits are privatised and environmental costs socialised, the country may record gold income while losing natural capital. Public restoration expenditure also diverts scarce resources from other development priorities, including healthcare, education and productive infrastructure.
Why Enforcement Alone Falls Short Arrests, excavator seizures and military operations remain necessary, particularly in protected forests and waterways. But illegal mining can persist when expected profits exceed production costs and the perceived risk of meaningful punishment. Enforcement targeted only at workers on mining sites also misses financiers, gold buyers and commercial intermediaries.
Success should therefore be judged not solely by arrests or confiscations, but by cleaner rivers, restored farmland and a sustained decline in destructive mining. Credible sanctions and enforceable rehabilitation liabilities must complement enforcement.
GoldBod: Turning Traceability into Economic Incentives The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) offers an opportunity to influence mining behaviour through market access. GoldBod already has a responsible-sourcing policy covering environmental compliance, pollution controls and supplier due diligence.
In August 2026, its Chief Executive Officer acknowledged that GoldBod could not yet establish what share of its purchases was responsibly mined, while announcing plans for a national gold-traceability system. The real policy test is not whether GoldBod can identify where gold originated, but whether it can verify how that gold was produced. GoldBod and its authorised buyers should purchase only from licensed mining operations whose environmental compliance has been independently verified. A licence alone is insufficient. Mine-level records should link each gold lot to its source, environmental permits, pollution-control performance and rehabilitation obligations. Serious violations should trigger suspension from authorised purchasing channels, subject to fair verification and review.
To prevent legally sourced gold from becoming a cover for illegally mined supplies, transactions should be cross-checked against plausible mine production and independently audited. Public reporting should disclose the proportion of GoldBod purchases traceable to environmentally compliant sources. Controls against smuggling and illicit buyers must accompany these measures.
This approach would reward responsible miners with formal market access while raising the commercial cost of pollution. Alongside accessible licensing, cleaner technologies and viable rural livelihoods, it would distinguish legitimate small-scale mining from destructive illegality.
Conclusion Galamsey is simultaneously a tragedy of the commons, a negative-externality problem and a test of economic governance. Ghana must protect waterways through enforcement, make polluters pay for restoration and ensure that public gold purchasing does not reward environmental destruction.
A nation does not become wealthier merely by extracting more gold. It becomes wealthier when the benefits of extraction exceed the full costs imposed on its people, productive land and future generations.
The author, Nana Eghan, PhD is an agricultural economist and private citizen who is a resident of Adenta, Greater Accra. He can be reached via nanaeghan@gmail.com
